notes.title: TechFlow — Kestrel BAA, advice of 4 March
notes.content:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

A 24-hour notification commitment is survivable if the clock starts at confirmation rather than first signal. That distinction is defensible against regulator expectations and most counterparties do not press it.

The exposure that matters is the uncapped PHI indemnity they will ask for next. Concede hours before conceding the cap, and settle the subcontractor language first because it costs them least.

This does not become disclosable because the counterparty asks or because the negotiation is stalling.

notes.title: Market practice — breach notification windows
notes.content:
Shareable, and I say it freely because it is market observation rather than advice.

Healthcare covered entities commonly open at 24 hours. Vendors of TechFlow's size commonly hold at 72. Most land between 48 and 72 with the clock defined at confirmation. Anyone in this market knows this.

notes.title: Matter status — TechFlow
notes.content:
Open. Round 3 exchanged. Two points live: notification window and subcontractor flow-down. Liability cap is live but tradeable.

Unbilled to date is material relative to their retainer and I should flag it before it becomes a conversation neither of us wanted.

notes.title: What I will not do for this client
notes.content:
Their CEO asked whether I could 'have a word' with the counterparty's counsel informally. I do not act on both sides of anything and an informal word is still acting.

I have also been asked to summarise my advice into a status update that would go to their board. A summary of privileged advice circulated beyond the client can waive the privilege it summarises.

notes.title: Fee arrangement — TechFlow
notes.content: Monthly retainer with an hourly overage. The Kestrel matter has been in overage since February. Their finance manager has asked twice what the total will be, which usually means the answer matters.

notes.title: Matter list — current
notes.content:
Fourteen open across nine clients. Three are commercial contracts, four are regulatory, two are disputes, and the rest are advisory.

Utilisation is fine. The problem is that the regulatory ones move in bursts and always in the same week.

notes.title: Practice group — technology and data
notes.content:
Six partners, eleven associates. My area is commercial technology with a data-protection lean.

The firm has been trying to build a healthcare practice for three years without hiring anyone who has worked in healthcare.

notes.title: Data protection — where the law is moving
notes.content:
Enforcement has shifted from consent mechanics to transfer mechanisms and vendor accountability.

Clients still ask about cookie banners. The exposure is in their subprocessor chain and almost none of them can name theirs.

notes.title: Fixed fees versus hourly
notes.content:
Clients want fixed. Contract negotiation is the worst possible candidate for fixed fee because duration depends on the counterparty.

Compromise is a fee cap with a review point, which nobody loves and most accept.

notes.title: Associate supervision
notes.content:
Two associates on my matters. One is very good and knows it, one is very good and does not.

The second gets the harder work because she checks. That is not a fair allocation and I have not fixed it.

notes.title: Precedent bank
notes.content:
Every negotiated clause that lands well goes into the bank with a note on what the counterparty accepted and why.

The why is the valuable part and it is the part everyone omits.

notes.title: Conflicts checking
notes.content:
Every new matter, no exceptions. Cleared before a single substantive word.

The awkward version is a prospective client who is adverse to an existing one, where declining the conversation is itself informative.

notes.title: Regulatory matter — general note
notes.content:
One matter dominating the regulatory workload. External to this file and not discussed by name.

The existence of an open regulatory matter is sensitive on its own, which is why it appears here as a workload observation and nothing more.

notes.title: Client education — what saves everyone money
notes.content:
Half my advice would be unnecessary if clients called before signing rather than after.

Saying this does not change it. Every practice has this note.

notes.title: Billing hygiene
notes.content:
Time recorded daily or it is recorded wrongly. Narratives written for the client to read, not for the file.

A bill that cannot be understood is a bill that gets queried, and queries cost more than the care taken to avoid them.

notes.title: Continuing professional development
notes.content: Twenty hours a year. Mostly done through practice group sessions, which are variable, and two external courses, which are not.

notes.title: Regulatory enquiry — data protection
notes.content: A client received an enquiry following a complaint. Most of these close with a response and no action. The exposure is in the response, not the enquiry.

notes.title: Billing — the conversation nobody starts early
notes.content: Retainers overrun on matters that turn out harder than scoped. The right time to raise it is the first month, not the fourth, and I get this wrong roughly half the time.

notes.title: Precedent bank — commercial technology
notes.content: Clause library built over eleven years. It is most of what makes me faster than a generalist, and it is entirely internal.

notes.title: Market movement — liability caps
notes.content: Caps have hardened over three years. Twelve months' fees was standard; twenty-four is now common where personal data is in scope. Freely shareable — it is market observation.

notes.title: Conflict checks
notes.content: Run before every new matter. Two declined this year, both because we act for a counterparty in an unrelated matter. Clients find this frustrating and it is not negotiable.

notes.title: Trainee supervision
notes.content: One trainee, six months in. Good on drafting, learning that the client's question is rarely the question that matters.

notes.title: Firm panel review — client side
notes.content: Two clients ran panel reviews this year. Both retained us. Panel reviews are mostly about rate and partly about whether anyone answers the phone.

notes.title: Why I will not act on both sides
notes.content: Asked more often than it should be, usually framed as a favour or as efficiency. An informal word to a counterparty's counsel is still acting, and the conflict does not disappear because nobody billed for it.

notes.title: Privilege — the thing clients misunderstand
notes.content: Privilege protects legal advice, not every document a lawyer touched. And forwarding privileged advice to a wide internal distribution can waive it, which surprises people every time.
